svg.aria-label: Diagram: the two pillars of a Google Cloud IAM design and the environment-first folder layout the security foundations blueprint uses, the documented fact that super admins can implicitly modify the organization IAM policy, why single sign-on being a global setting requires a separate staging directory account, and the assembled design decisions with the post that established each
svg.title: An IAM design for a multi-team organisation, assembled from twenty-nine posts
svg.text: Two pillars, one directory, environment-first folders — and one account above all of it.
Including a correction to #55: the super admin does not merely sit beside the IAM plane, it reaches into it.
Two pillars, and the layout the blueprint actually uses
Directory: Cloud Identity and Workspace accounts are containers for users and groups.
Hierarchy: organizations are containers for projects and resources. Lower levels INHERIT.
Folders group projects by ENVIRONMENT, not by team: bootstrap, common, networking,
development, nonproduction, production. Teams get projects inside them.
The correction to #55: super admin reaches INTO the IAM plane
Super admins are IMPLICITLY granted permission to modify the IAM policy of the organization node.
That lets them assign themselves organization administrator, or any other role.
They can also delete the account, its Google Cloud organization, and all its resources.
Google states the conclusion: assume super admins have full access to everything.
Which is why staging needs its own directory account
Enabling single sign-on is a GLOBAL setting applying to all users other than super admins.
There is no per-user rollout for it, unlike almost every other Workspace setting.
And an IdP misconfiguration can leave users modified, suspended, or even DELETED.
So: separate staging and production directory accounts, each paired with its own IdP.
The design, as one list — with the post that established each line
One directory account: as few as possible, as many as necessary
Access groups per job function; not org groups, never nested
Post-SSO verification on; Google 2SV on every super admin
Two to five break-glass accounts, hardware keys, split custody
PAM entitlements over standing roles; non-authoritative Terraform
An aggregated audit sink into a dedicated logging project
Do NOT separate Workspace from Google Cloud to contain super admins. Duplicating users hurts
experience and admin overhead, and that Cloud Identity domain cannot route notification email.
Twenty-nine posts, one design. Every layer is sound; several answer a narrower question than
their name implies; and one account sits above all of it by construction, not by error.
